      <content name="title">Head and <span class="qt0">Neck</span> Cancer</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer? <p>Head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer is the name for cancers that develop in the mouth, nose and sinuses, salivary glands, and throat and voice box (larynx). Most head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancers are squamous cell cancers. They begin in the moist tissues that line the head and <span class="qt0">neck</span>. The cancer cells may spread into deeper tissue as the cancer grows.</p><p>There are other cancers that develop in the head and <span class="qt0">neck</span>, such as brain cancer, eye cancer, and esophageal cancer. But they are usually not considered to be head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancers, because those types of cancer and their treatments are different.</p>Who is more likely to develop head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer? <p>Anyone can get head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer, but you are more likely to develop it if you:</p><ul><li>Use tobacco or drink lots of alcohol. Your risk of developing head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer is even higher if you do both.</li><li>Are male.</li><li>Are over age 50.</li><li>Have a history of head or <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer.</li><li>Have HPV (for cancers in the tonsils and base of the tongue).</li><li>Are exposed to wood dusts or certain other toxic substances at work (for upper throat, nose, and sinus cancers).</li><li>Have had radiation exposure to the head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> (for salivary gland cancer).</li><li>Have Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection (for upper throat and salivary gland cancers).</li><li>Are Asian (for upper throat cancer).</li></ul>What are the symptoms of head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer?<p>The symptoms of head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer may include:</p><ul><li>A lump in the <span class="qt0">neck</span></li><li>A sore in the mouth or the throat that does not heal and may be painful</li><li>A sore throat that does not go away</li><li>Trouble swallowing</li><li>A change or hoarseness in the voice</li></ul><p>Other possible symptoms can depend on the specific type of head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer.</p>How is head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer diagnosed?<p>Which exams and tests used to diagnose head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer can depend on the specific type of cancer. Possible exams and tests may include:</p><ul><li>A physical exam of the area that might have cancer.</li><li>Blood and/or urine tests.</li><li>An endoscopy.</li><li>A biopsy or other procedure to collect cells from the area that might have cancer. The cells are viewed under a microscope to find out if they are abnormal.</li><li>Imaging tests.</li></ul>What are the treatments for head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer?<p>The treatment for head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer will depend on the specific type of cancer, the stage (how advanced the cancer is), your overall health, and other factors. The treatment options might include:</p><ul><li>Surgery</li><li>Radiation therapy</li><li>Chemotherapy</li><li>Cancer immunotherapy</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that mainly attack specific cancer cells and cause less harm to normal cells</li></ul><p>In some cases, you may need a combination of treatments. Sometimes surgery can affect how well you can chew, swallow, or talk. Rehabilitation, such as physical therapy, dietary counseling, and speech therapy, may help.</p>Can head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer be prevented?<p>There are steps you can take to help prevent head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer:</p><ul><li>Not smoking</li><li>Limiting alcohol use or not drinking at all</li><li>Getting regular dental exams</li><li>Talking to your provider about HPV vaccination</li></ul><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/neckinjuriesanddisorders.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Neck</span> Injuries and Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cervical Spine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Whiplash</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Any part of your <span class="qt0">neck</span> - muscles, bones, joints, tendons, ligaments, or nerves - can cause <span class="qt0">neck</span> problems. <span class="qt0">Neck</span> pain is very common. Pain may also come from your shoulder, jaw, head, or upper arms. </p><p>Muscle strain or tension often causes <span class="qt0">neck</span> pain. The problem is usually overuse, such as from sitting at a computer for too long.  Sometimes you can strain your <span class="qt0">neck</span> muscles from sleeping in an awkward position or overdoing it during exercise. Falls or accidents, including car accidents, are another common cause of <span class="qt0">neck</span> pain.  Whiplash, a soft tissue injury to the <span class="qt0">neck</span>, is also called <span class="qt0">neck</span> sprain or strain.</p><p>Treatment depends on the cause, but may include applying ice, taking pain relievers, getting physical therapy or wearing a cervical collar. You rarely need surgery.</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/oralcancer.html">
      <content name="title">Oral Cancer</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Mouth Cancer</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Tongue Cancer</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is oral cancer? <p>Oral cancer is cancer of the mouth. It is a type of head and <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer. Most oral cancers are squamous cell cancers. They begin in the flat cells that cover the surfaces of your mouth, tongue, and lips. The cancer cells may spread into deeper tissue as the cancer grows.</p><p>Most oral cancers are related to tobacco use, heavy alcohol use, or an HPV infection.</p>Who is more likely to develop oral cancer?<p>Anyone can get oral cancer, but you are more likely to develop it if you:</p><ul><li>Use tobacco or drink lots of alcohol. Your risk of developing oral cancer is even higher if you do both.</li><li>Are male.</li><li>Are over ago 40.</li><li>Have HPV.</li><li>Have a history of head or <span class="qt0">neck</span> cancer.</li><li>Get frequent sun exposure (for lip cancer).</li></ul>What are the symptoms of oral cancer?<p>The symptoms of oral cancer may include:</p><ul><li>A white or red patch in your mouth</li><li>A lip or mouth sore that won't heal</li><li>Bleeding, pain, or numbness in the lip or mouth</li><li>Loose teeth or dentures that no longer fit well</li><li>Problems or pain with swallowing</li><li>A lump in your <span class="qt0">neck</span></li><li>Ear pain</li><li>Trouble moving your mouth or jaw</li><li>Swelling of the jaw</li><li>A sore throat or feeling that something is caught in the throat</li></ul><p>If you have any of these symptoms for more than two weeks, see your health care provider or dentist. Oral cancer can spread quickly, so it's important to find it early.</p>How is oral cancer diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have oral cancer, your provider may use:</p><ul><li>A physical exam of the lips and mouth.</li><li>An endoscopy.</li><li>A biopsy or other procedure to collect cells from the lip or oral cavity. The cells are viewed under a microscope to find out if they are abnormal.</li><li>Imaging tests.</li></ul>What are the treatments for oral cancer?<p>The treatments for oral cancer include surgery, radiation therapy, or both. After surgery, some people also need chemotherapy to kill any cancer cells that are left.</p>Can oral cancer be prevented?<p>There are steps you can take to help prevent oral cancer:</p><ul><li>Not smoking</li><li>Limiting alcohol use or not drinking at all</li><li>Getting regular dental exams</li></ul><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/guidetogoodposture.html">
      <content name="title">Guide to Good Posture</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Posture</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Good posture is about more than standing up straight so you can look your best. It is an important part of your long-term health. Making sure that you hold your body the right way, whether you are moving or still, can prevent pain, injuries, and other health problems.</p>What is posture?<p>Posture is how you hold your body. There are two types:</p><ul><li>Dynamic posture is how you hold yourself when you are moving, like when you are walking, running, or bending over to pick up something.</li><li>Static posture is how you hold yourself when you are not moving, like when you are sitting, standing, or sleeping.</li></ul><p>It is important to make sure that you have good dynamic and static posture.</p><p>The key to good posture is the position of your spine. Your spine has three natural curves - at your <span class="qt0">neck</span>, mid back, and low back. Correct posture should maintain these curves, but not increase them. Your head should be above your shoulders, and the top of your shoulder should be over the hips.</p>How can posture affect my health?<p>Poor posture can be bad for your health. Slouching or slumping over can:</p><ul><li>Misalign your musculoskeletal system</li><li>Wear away at your spine, making it more fragile and prone to injury</li><li>Cause <span class="qt0">neck</span>, shoulder, and back pain</li><li>Decrease your flexibility</li><li>Affect how well your joints move</li><li>Affect your balance and increase your risk of falling</li><li>Make it harder to digest your food</li><li>Make it harder to breathe</li></ul>How can I improve my posture in general?<p>
</p><ul><li>Be mindful of your posture during everyday activities, like watching television, washing dishes, or walking</li><li>Stay active. Any kind of exercise may help improve your posture, but certain types of exercises can be especially helpful. They include yoga, tai chi, and other classes that focus on body awareness. It is also a good idea to do exercises that strengthen your core (muscles around your back, abdomen, and pelvis).</li><li>Maintain a healthy weight. Extra weight can weaken your abdominal muscles, cause problems for your pelvis and spine, and contribute to low back pain. All of these can hurt your posture.</li><li>Wear comfortable, low-heeled shoes. High heels, for example, can throw off your balance and force you to walk differently. This puts more stress on your muscles and harms your posture.</li><li>Make sure work surfaces are at a comfortable height for you, whether you're sitting in front of a computer, making dinner, or eating a meal.</li></ul>How can I improve my posture when sitting?<p>Many Americans spend a lot of their time sitting - either at work, at school, or at home. It is important to sit properly, and to take frequent breaks:</p><ul><li>Switch sitting positions often</li><li>Take brief walks around your office or home</li><li>Gently stretch your muscles every so often to help relieve muscle tension</li><li>Don't cross your legs; keep your feet on the floor, with your ankles in front of your knees</li><li>Make sure that your feet touch the floor, or if that's not possible, use a footrest</li><li>Relax your shoulders; they should not be rounded or pulled backwards</li><li>Keep your elbows in close to your body. They should be bent between 90 and 120 degrees.</li><li>Make sure that your back is fully supported. Use a back pillow or other back support if your chair does not have a backrest that can support your lower back's curve.</li><li>Make sure that your thighs and hips are supported. You should have a well-padded seat, and your thighs and hips should be parallel to the floor.</li></ul>How can I improve my posture when standing?<p>
</p><ul><li>Stand up straight and tall</li><li>Keep your shoulders back</li><li>Pull your stomach in</li><li>Put your weight mostly on the balls of your feet</li><li>Keep your head level</li><li>Let your arms hang down naturally at your sides</li><li>Keep your feet about shoulder-width apart</li></ul><p>With practice, you can improve your posture; you will look and feel better.</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/thyroidcancer.html">
      <content name="title">Thyroid Cancer</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is thyroid cancer?<p>Thyroid cancer is a cancer that starts in the tissues of the thyroid. Your thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped gland in the front of your <span class="qt0">neck</span>. It makes hormones that control the way the body uses energy. These hormones affect nearly every organ in your body and control many of your body's most important functions. For example, they affect your breathing, heart rate, weight, digestion, and moods.</p>What are the different types of thyroid cancer?<p>There are different types of thyroid cancer; the main ones include:</p><ul><li>Differentiated thyroid cancer, which includes papillary cancer and follicular cancer</li><li>Medullary thyroid cancer</li><li>Anaplastic thyroid cancer</li></ul>Who is more likely to develop thyroid cancer?<p>Certain people are more likely to develop thyroid cancer. Your risk is higher if you:</p><ul><li>Are between ages 25 and 65</li><li>Are a woman</li><li>Are Asian</li><li>Were exposed to certain types of radiation, including from radiation treatments to your head or <span class="qt0">neck</span> as a child or from a radiation emergency</li><li>Have had a goiter (enlarged thyroid)</li><li>Having certain genetic conditions, including certain types of multiple endocrine neoplasia</li><li>Have a family history of thyroid cancer or thyroid disease</li></ul>What are the symptoms of thyroid cancer?<p>Thyroid cancer may not cause symptoms at first. It is sometimes found during a routine physical exam. You may get signs or symptoms as the cancer gets bigger. The symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>A lump (nodule) in the <span class="qt0">neck</span></li><li>Trouble breathing</li><li>Trouble swallowing</li><li>Pain when swallowing</li><li>Hoarseness or other changes to your voice that do not get better</li></ul>How is thyroid cancer diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have thyroid cancer, your health care provider may use:</p><ul><li>A physical exam, including checking your <span class="qt0">neck</span> for swelling, lumps, or anything that seems unusual</li><li>A medical history</li><li>Thyroid tests</li><li>Other blood or imaging tests</li><li>A biopsy</li></ul>What are the treatments for thyroid cancer?<p>Treatment for thyroid cancer depends on the type of cancer you have and whether the cancer has spread. Often, more than one type of treatment may be needed. The treatment options include:</p><ul><li>Surgery.</li><li>Radiation therapy, including radioactive iodine therapy.</li><li>Chemotherapy.</li><li>Thyroid hormone therapy.</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that attack specific cancer cells with less harm to normal cells.</li><li>Watchful waiting, which means that you don't get treatment right away. Your regularly checks to see if your signs or symptoms appear or change.</li></ul><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>
